title: Extradural haematoma at the pterion
text:
The pterion, where frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet, is the thinnest part of the lateral skull. A blow here tears the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery running in a groove on its inner surface. Arterial blood strips the dura from the skull, forming a biconvex (lentiform) haematoma that does not cross suture lines.
Classically there is a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration, ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil from uncal herniation compressing the oculomotor nerve, and contralateral hemiparesis. Urgent burr-hole decompression saves lives.

title: Subdural haematoma and venous sinus thrombosis
text:
Bridging veins crossing the subdural space to the superior sagittal sinus tear with acceleration-deceleration, especially in the elderly and alcohol users (brain atrophy stretches them) and in shaken infants. The crescent-shaped haematoma crosses sutures; chronic subdurals present with fluctuating confusion weeks later.
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (pregnancy, oral contraceptive, dehydration, thrombophilia, mastoiditis spreading to the sigmoid sinus) causes headache, papilloedema, seizures and venous haemorrhagic infarction.

title: Cavernous sinus thrombosis and carotid-cavernous fistula
text:
The facial 'danger triangle' drains through valveless ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus, so infection of the nose or upper lip (or sphenoid sinusitis) can cause septic thrombosis: fever, proptosis, chemosis and ophthalmoplegia. The abducens nerve (VI) lies free within the sinus beside the internal carotid artery and is usually affected first; oculomotor, trochlear and the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve lie in the lateral wall.
A carotid-cavernous fistula (trauma or ruptured aneurysm) causes pulsatile exophthalmos with an orbital bruit.

title: Bell palsy versus a central facial lesion
text:
A lower motor neurone lesion of the facial nerve (Bell palsy, likely HSV reactivation causing swelling within the narrow facial canal) paralyses the whole half of the face, including forehead wrinkling and eye closure. Proximal lesions also cause hyperacusis (nerve to stapedius), loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani) and dry eye (greater petrosal nerve), which helps localise the lesion.
An upper motor neurone lesion (stroke) spares the forehead, because the part of the facial nucleus supplying the upper face receives bilateral cortical input.
Other causes: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV, vesicles in the ear), parotid tumours, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, temporal bone fractures and acoustic neuroma.

title: Parotid tumours and the facial nerve
text:
About 80% of salivary tumours arise in the parotid and most are benign: pleomorphic adenoma (recurs if its capsule is breached) and Warthin tumour (smokers, often bilateral). A parotid mass with facial nerve palsy suggests malignancy such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma. The facial nerve divides into its five branches within the gland, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes, and is at risk during parotidectomy.
Frey syndrome after surgery: regenerating parasympathetic fibres from the auriculotemporal nerve innervate sweat glands, causing gustatory sweating. Mumps causes painful bilateral parotitis.

title: Sialolithiasis and Ludwig angina
text:
Most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland: its secretion is more mucous and alkaline, and the long duct runs uphill against gravity. Pain and swelling on eating are classic.
Ludwig angina is a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, usually from infected lower molars whose roots lie below the mylohyoid line. The floor of the mouth and tongue are pushed up and back, threatening the airway.

title: Thyroid surgery hazards and thyroid disease
text:
The recurrent laryngeal nerves run in the tracheo-oesophageal groove close to the inferior thyroid artery; unilateral injury gives hoarseness, bilateral injury can cause stridor and airway obstruction. The external laryngeal nerve accompanies the superior thyroid artery and its injury causes loss of high-pitched voice (cricothyroid paralysis). Inadvertent removal of the parathyroids causes hypocalcaemia and tetany.
Graves disease (TSH receptor antibodies) causes hyperthyroidism, pretibial myxoedema and exophthalmos; Hashimoto thyroiditis causes hypothyroidism and raises the risk of thyroid lymphoma. Papillary carcinoma (psammoma bodies, Orphan Annie nuclei) spreads to cervical nodes; follicular carcinoma spreads by blood to bone and lung; medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-producing C cells in MEN2.
A thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck lump that rises on protruding the tongue.

title: Hyperparathyroidism
text:
A single parathyroid adenoma is the usual cause of primary hyperparathyroidism: 'bones, stones, groans and psychic moans' (osteitis fibrosa cystica with subperiosteal resorption of the phalanges, renal calculi, constipation and pancreatitis, depression). Secondary hyperparathyroidism follows chronic kidney disease.
The inferior parathyroids develop from the third pharyngeal pouch together with the thymus and migrate further, so ectopic glands may lie in the thymus or mediastinum; the superior glands derive from the fourth pouch and are more constant in position.

title: Pituitary adenoma and bitemporal hemianopia
text:
The pituitary sits in the sella turcica directly below the optic chiasm. A macroadenoma growing upward compresses the crossing nasal retinal fibres, causing bitemporal hemianopia (typically beginning in the upper temporal quadrants). Lateral growth invades the cavernous sinus.
Functioning adenomas: prolactinoma (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, erectile dysfunction), GH (acromegaly, gigantism in children), ACTH (Cushing disease). Sheehan syndrome is postpartum infarction of the enlarged anterior pituitary after haemorrhage; pituitary apoplexy is sudden haemorrhage into a tumour. Damage to the posterior pituitary or stalk causes central diabetes insipidus. Craniopharyngioma, from Rathke pouch remnants, is the suprasellar calcified childhood equivalent.

title: Tonsillitis, quinsy and tonsillectomy bleeding
text:
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) forms between the tonsillar capsule and superior constrictor, deviating the uvula to the opposite side with trismus and a 'hot potato' voice. Infection can spread to the parapharyngeal space, near the internal carotid artery and jugular vein.
Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage usually comes from the external palatine (paratonsillar) vein; the internal carotid artery lies about 2.5 cm posterolateral. Ear pain after tonsillectomy is referred via the glossopharyngeal nerve (tympanic branch).

title: Laryngeal airway: cricothyroidotomy, epiglottitis and cancer
text:
In a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' emergency, the airway is entered through the median cricothyroid ligament, palpable just below the thyroid cartilage prominence. The cricoid is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway.
Acute epiglottitis (historically Haemophilus influenzae type b) causes drooling, a tripod posture and a 'thumbprint' sign on lateral X-ray; examining the throat can precipitate obstruction.
Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the glottis (vocal cords) presents early with hoarseness and rarely spreads to nodes, because the vocal cords have almost no lymphatic drainage; supraglottic tumours metastasise early.

title: The only vocal cord abductor
text:
Posterior crico-arytenoid is the only muscle that opens the rima glottidis. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy leaves both cords near the midline: the voice may be reasonably good but breathing is compromised with stridor, often requiring tracheostomy.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch, so aortic aneurysm, left hilar lung cancer, mitral stenosis (enlarged left atrium) and mediastinal nodes can cause left vocal cord palsy and hoarseness.

title: Vagus nerve lesions and the recurrent laryngeal nerve
text:
A vagal lesion (jugular foramen tumour, brainstem stroke such as lateral medullary syndrome) causes uvular deviation AWAY from the lesion, palatal weakness with nasal speech and regurgitation, dysphagia, loss of the gag reflex (efferent limb) and an ipsilateral paralysed vocal cord.
Jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet) combines IX, X and XI palsies.
The recurrent laryngeal branches are the part most often injured: thyroid surgery on either side, and aortic arch or left lung pathology on the left.

title: Hypoglossal nerve palsy
text: A lower motor neurone lesion causes ipsilateral tongue wasting and fasciculation, and the protruded tongue deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion (the intact genioglossus pushes it over). Causes include carotid endarterectomy, internal carotid dissection, skull base tumours and motor neurone disease (bulbar palsy). Medial medullary syndrome combines XII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis and loss of proprioception.

title: Third nerve palsy: surgical versus medical
text:
Complete palsy: ptosis, the eye rests 'down and out' (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique), and a fixed dilated pupil.
Parasympathetic pupillary fibres travel on the outside of the nerve, so compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm or uncal herniation affects the pupil early ('surgical third'), and needs urgent imaging. Diabetic microvascular infarction affects the core of the nerve and typically spares the pupil ('medical third').

title: Abducens palsy as a false localising sign
text:
The abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course, stretched over the petrous apex, so raised intracranial pressure from any cause (tumour, idiopathic intracranial hypertension) can produce unilateral or bilateral lateral rectus palsy, a 'false localising' sign. Horizontal diplopia is worse looking toward the affected side.
A lesion of the abducens nucleus itself causes a horizontal gaze palsy (it contains interneurons to the contralateral medial rectus via the medial longitudinal fasciculus) and often an ipsilateral facial palsy, as the facial fibres loop around it.

title: Trochlear palsy
text: The only cranial nerve to exit dorsally and to decussate, with a long thin course that makes it vulnerable to head trauma. Superior oblique weakness causes vertical diplopia worse on looking down and inward (reading, descending stairs); patients tilt their head away from the affected side to compensate.

title: Trigeminal neuralgia and herpes zoster ophthalmicus
text:
Trigeminal neuralgia: paroxysms of electric-shock pain in the maxillary or mandibular territory, triggered by chewing, shaving or wind, most often from a looping superior cerebellar artery compressing the root entry zone (treated with carbamazepine or microvascular decompression). In young patients, consider multiple sclerosis.
Herpes zoster in the ophthalmic division: vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign, nasociliary branch) predict eye involvement and threaten sight.

title: Papilloedema, optic neuritis and retinal artery occlusion
text:
The optic nerve is surrounded by meningeal sheaths continuous with the subarachnoid space, so raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc (papilloedema).
Optic neuritis (often the first presentation of multiple sclerosis) causes painful loss of vision, colour desaturation and a relative afferent pupillary defect.
Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless monocular blindness with a pale retina and cherry-red spot at the fovea; giant cell arteritis must be excluded. Central retinal vein occlusion causes 'blood and thunder' haemorrhages.

title: Cataract and lens dislocation
text:
Cataract is opacification of the lens with age, diabetes, corticosteroids, radiation or congenital infection (rubella). Congenital cataract abolishes the red reflex and causes amblyopia if not treated early.
Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) is superotemporal in Marfan syndrome (weak fibrillin in the zonular fibres) and inferonasal in homocystinuria.

title: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
text: In a shallow anterior chamber (hypermetropia, older age), a mid-dilated iris blocks the drainage angle and aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm. Intraocular pressure rises abruptly: painful red eye, halos around lights, hazy cornea from oedema, fixed mid-dilated pupil, headache and vomiting. Anticholinergic drugs or dim light can precipitate it. Laser iridotomy creates an alternative channel.

title: Otitis media, otosclerosis and hearing loss
text:
Acute otitis media causes a red, bulging tympanic membrane; complications include perforation, mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy (the nerve passes through the middle ear wall) and meningitis. Chronic cholesteatoma erodes the ossicles.
Otosclerosis fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, causing progressive conductive deafness in young adults (Rinne negative, Weber lateralises to the affected ear).
Sensorineural loss from the cochlea: noise damage (4 kHz notch), presbycusis (high frequencies), aminoglycosides, Ménière disease (endolymphatic hydrops with vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating low-frequency loss).

title: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
text:
A benign Schwann cell tumour of the vestibular nerve at the cerebellopontine angle causes unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, then compresses the trigeminal nerve (loss of corneal reflex), facial nerve and eventually the cerebellum and brainstem. Bilateral tumours are diagnostic of neurofibromatosis type 2.
Vestibular neuritis causes acute vertigo without hearing loss; benign paroxysmal positional vertigo arises from otoconia displaced into the posterior semicircular canal.

title: Mandibular fracture and dislocation
text:
The mandible and its ring with the temporomandibular joints often breaks in two places (e.g. angle on one side and parasymphysis or condyle on the other). Fractures through the angle are pulled apart by masseter and medial pterygoid. Injury to the inferior alveolar nerve in its canal numbs the lower lip and chin.
Anterior dislocation of the temporomandibular joint occurs with yawning: the condyle slips in front of the articular eminence and spasm of the muscles of mastication locks the mouth open.

title: Midface and orbital floor fractures
text:
Le Fort I (horizontal above the teeth), II (pyramidal through the nasal bridge and orbital floor) and III (craniofacial disjunction) fractures follow lines of weakness of the midface; II and III can cause CSF rhinorrhoea.
A blow to the eye can 'blow out' the thin orbital floor into the maxillary sinus, trapping inferior rectus (restricted upward gaze, diplopia) and injuring the infraorbital nerve (numb cheek and upper lip). Zygomatic 'tripod' fractures flatten the cheek and can cause trismus if the arch impinges on the coronoid process.

title: Carotid stenosis and dissection
text:
Atherosclerosis concentrates at the carotid bifurcation and origin of the internal carotid artery, where turbulent flow occurs. Emboli cause transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax, via the ophthalmic artery), TIAs and middle cerebral artery strokes; symptomatic stenosis over 50-70% is treated by carotid endarterectomy, which risks the hypoglossal and vagus nerves.
Internal carotid dissection (minor neck trauma, chiropractic manipulation, connective tissue disease) causes neck pain, Horner syndrome (sympathetic fibres run on the artery) and delayed stroke.
Pressure on the carotid sinus causes reflex bradycardia and hypotension (carotid sinus hypersensitivity).

title: Jugular venous access and Lemierre syndrome
text:
The internal jugular vein, lateral to the common carotid within the carotid sheath, is a standard central line route, usually via the right side (straighter path to the SVC, avoids the thoracic duct). The apex of the triangle between the two heads of sternocleidomastoid is the landmark; complications include carotid puncture and pneumothorax.
The external jugular vein is visible and used to estimate venous pressure crudely.
Lemierre syndrome: septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after pharyngitis (Fusobacterium necrophorum) with septic pulmonary emboli.

title: Congenital muscular torticollis
text:
Fibrosis and shortening of sternocleidomastoid in infants (possibly birth trauma or intrauterine positioning; a palpable 'tumour' in the muscle) tilts the head toward and rotates the chin away from the affected side. Untreated, it causes facial and skull asymmetry (plagiocephaly). Most respond to stretching.
Spasmodic torticollis (cervical dystonia) in adults is treated with botulinum toxin.

title: Accessory nerve injury in the posterior triangle
text: The spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck superficially, embedded in the investing fascia, and is the commonest iatrogenic nerve injury during lymph node biopsy there. Trapezius paralysis causes shoulder droop, aching and difficulty abducting above 90° with lateral winging of the scapula. Sternocleidomastoid is usually spared because its branch arises before the nerve crosses the triangle.

title: Jefferson, hangman and odontoid fractures
text:
Jefferson fracture: axial load (diving) bursts the ring of the atlas; spreading of the lateral masses is visible on open-mouth views and neurological injury is uncommon because the canal widens.
Hangman fracture: bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis of the axis from hyperextension (judicial hanging, dashboard injury), producing traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.
Odontoid (dens) fractures in elderly falls; type II through the base has a high non-union rate. The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens; laxity in rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome allows atlantoaxial subluxation with cord compression.

title: Dental abscess spread
text:
Periapical abscesses spread according to root position relative to muscle attachments. Lower molar roots below the mylohyoid line drain to the submandibular space (Ludwig angina risk); upper molar and premolar infections can enter the maxillary sinus (odontogenic sinusitis) or, via facial veins, the cavernous sinus. Maxillary canine infections may track to the orbit.
Inferior alveolar nerve blocks deposit anaesthetic at the mandibular foramen; an injection placed too posteriorly enters the parotid gland and causes transient facial palsy.
